title: Shaquille O'Neal
description: American former basketball player and sports analyst (born 1972)
wiki_lead:
Shaquille Rashaun O'Neal (born March 6, 1972), often referred to by his nickname "Shaq", is an American former professional basketball player who is a sports analyst. A 7-foot-1-inch (2.16 m) center, O'Neal played for six different teams over his 19-year career in the National Basketball Association (NBA). He is a four-time NBA champion, three-time NBA Finals MVP, and the 2000 NBA MVP. He is widely regarded as one of the most dominant centers in NBA history and one of the greatest basketball players of all time. 
After playing college basketball for the LSU Tigers, O'Neal was selected by the Orlando Magic with the first overall pick in the 1992 NBA draft. He was named NBA Rookie of the Year in 1992–93 and led his team to the 1995 NBA Finals. After four years with the Magic, O'Neal signed as a free agent with the Los Angeles Lakers. He and the Lakers won the NBA championship in 2000, 2001, and 2002. Amid a feud between O'Neal and his teammate Kobe Bryant, O'Neal was traded in 2004 to the Miami Heat, where he won his fourth NBA championship in 2006. During the last several years of his career he spent short stints with the Phoenix Suns, the Cleveland Cavaliers and the Boston Celtics.
O'Neal's accolades include 15 All-Star Game selections, three All-Star Game MVP awards, 14 All-NBA team selections, three NBA All-Defensive Team selections and two scoring titles. He is one of three players to be named NBA MVP, All-Star Game MVP and Finals MVP in the same year. He ranks 9th all-time in points scored, 6th in field goals, 15th in rebounds, and 8th in blocks. He had a 58.2% career field goal percentage and led the league in field goal percentage ten times. He is a member of the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame and the FIBA Hall of Fame, and was named to the NBA 50th Anniversary Team and the NBA 75th Anniversary Team as one of the greatest players in league history.
In addition to his basketball career, O'Neal has released four rap albums, including the platinum-certified Shaq Diesel (1993) and the gold-certified Shaq Fu: Da Return (1994). Under the name Diesel, he produces electronic music and tours as a DJ. He has appeared in numerous films and has starred in reality shows such as Shaq Vs. and Shaq's Big Challenge. O'Neal is the general manager of the Sacramento State Hornets men's basketball team.

O'Neal is the general manager of the Sacramento State Hornets men's basketball team.


Early life
Shaquille Rashaun O'Neal was born on March 6, 1972, in Newark, New Jersey, to Joe Toney and Lucille O'Neal. Toney had played high school basketball and was offered a scholarship to play at Seton Hall. He struggled with drug addiction and was imprisoned for drug possession when O'Neal was an infant. Upon his release, he did not resume a place in O'Neal's life and relinquished his parental rights to O'Neal's stepfather, Phillip Arthur Harrison, a career Army sergeant. O'Neal remained estranged from Toney for decades and was not interested in establishing a relationship. In his 1994 single "Biological Didn't Bother", O'Neal called Harrison his father. Harrison died of a heart attack in 2013. O'Neal met Toney for the first time in 2016.
O'Neal's family moved many times during his childhood, sometimes staying with relatives, including O'Neal's grandmother in Jersey City. In addition to living in multiple cities in New Jersey, the family also lived in Georgia, Texas and Germany. In his 2002 autobiography, O'Neal wrote that he still considers Newark his home. He credited the Boys & Girls Clubs of America in Newark with keeping him off the streets during his youth and giving him a safe place to play basketball. O'Neal's mother is Baptist and his stepfather was Muslim, and they taught him both religions.
O'Neal's parents were both over 6 feet (1.83 meters) tall, and by age thirteen O'Neal was 6 ft 6 in (1.98 m) tall. He played basketball at Robert G. Cole High School in San Antonio, Texas, leading his team to a 68–1 record over two years and winning the state championship during his senior year. His 791 rebounds during the 1988-89 season remains a Texas record for a high school player. O'Neal wore the No. 33 jersey in high school because he admired Patrick Ewing, who wore 33. O'Neal's high school basketball team retired the No. 33 in 2014.


College career
After graduating from high school in 1989, O'Neal studied business at Louisiana State University (LSU), where he joined the Theta Kappa chapter of Omega Psi Phi fraternity. He played basketball for the LSU Tigers under coach Dale Brown, whom he had met years earlier at the U.S. Army base in Wildflecken, West Germany, where his stepfather was stationed. While playing for LSU, O'Neal was a two-time All-American, two-time SEC Player of the Year, and received the Adolph Rupp Trophy as NCAA men's basketball player of the year in 1991. He was also named college player of the year by the Associated Press and UPI. O'Neal left LSU after three years to pursue his NBA career, but later returned to the university, earning a bachelor's degree in general studies with a minor in political science in 2000. He was later inducted into the LSU Hall of Fame. A 900-pound (410 kg) bronze statue of O'Neal is located in front of the LSU Basketball Practice Facility.


Professional career


Orlando Magic (1992–1996)
The Orlando Magic selected O'Neal with the 1st overall pick in the 1992 NBA draft. In the summer before moving to Orlando, Florida, O'Neal spent time in Los Angeles under the tutelage of Hall of Famer Magic Johnson. When joining the Magic, he chose the No. 32 jersey because his veteran teammate Terry Catledge wore No. 33. O'Neal became the first NBA player to be named the Player of the Week in his first week in the league. During his rookie season, he averaged 23.4 points on 56.2% shooting, 13.9 rebounds, and 3.5 blocks per game. He was named the 1993 NBA Rookie of the Year and was the first rookie to be named an All-Star starter since Michael Jordan in 1985. The Magic finished the season 41–41, winning 20 more games than the previous season, but missed the playoffs via a tie-breaker with the Indiana Pacers. According to Sports Illustrated writer Jack McCallum, O'Neal wanted head coach Matty Guokas to be replaced by assistant coach Brian Hill.
In 1993–1994, O'Neal's second season, Hill served as coach and Guokas was reassigned to the front office. O'Neal improved his scoring average to 29.3 points (second in the league behind David Robinson) while leading the NBA in field goal percentage at 60%. On November 20, 1993, against the New Jersey Nets, O'Neal registered the first triple-double of his career, recording 24 points to go along with career highs of 28 rebounds and 15 blocks. He was selected for the All-Star game and the All-NBA 3rd Team. The Magic finished the season with a record of 50–32 and made the playoffs for the first time in franchise history. In his first playoff series, O'Neal averaged 20.7 points and 13.3 rebounds as the Magic were swept by the Pacers.
In O'Neal's third season, 1994–95, he led the NBA in scoring with a 29.3 point average. He finished second in MVP voting behind David Robinson and played in his third straight All-Star Game. O'Neal and Penny Hardaway formed one of the league's top duos and helped the Magic to a 57–25 record and the Atlantic Division title. The Magic won its first-ever playoff series against the Boston Celtics in the 1995 NBA playoffs, then defeated the Chicago Bulls in the conference semifinals and the Pacers in the conference finals. In the NBA Finals, the Magic faced the defending champion Houston Rockets, led by future Hall of Famers Hakeem Olajuwon and Clyde Drexler. During the Finals, O'Neal averaged 28 points on 59.5% shooting, 12.5 rebounds, and 6.3 assists; the Rockets swept the Magic in four games.
O'Neal missed 28 games during the 1995–96 season due to injuries. He averaged 26.6 points and 11 rebounds per game, made the All-NBA 3rd Team, and played in his fourth All-Star Game. The Magic finished with a regular season record of 60–22, second in the Eastern conference behind the Chicago Bulls, who finished with an NBA record 72 wins. The Magic defeated the Detroit Pistons and the Atlanta Hawks in the first two rounds of the 1996 NBA Playoffs, but were swept by the Bulls in the Eastern Conference finals.


Los Angeles Lakers (1996–2004)

O'Neal became a free agent after the 1995–96 NBA season. While he was weighing his options during the summer of 1996, and amid an ongoing power struggle between him and coach Brian Hill, the Orlando Sentinel published a poll asking whether the Magic should fire Hill if that were one of O'Neal's conditions for staying with the team, and whether O'Neal was worth the $115 million the Magic had offered him. The vast majority of respondents replied "no" to both questions. O'Neal was reportedly upset by the poll results and by earlier assertions in the Orlando media that he was not a good role model because he had a child with his longtime girlfriend with no immediate plans to marry.
At the 1996 Olympics in Atlanta, O'Neal and the U.S. Olympic basketball team won the gold medal. Near the start of the Olympics, it was announced that O'Neal would join the Los Angeles Lakers on a seven-year, $121 million contract. O'Neal insisted he did not choose the Lakers for the money. He switched his jersey to No. 34, as the No. 32 jersey he had worn in Orlando had been retired by the Lakers in honor of Magic Johnson, and the No. 33 jersey he had worn at LSU had been retired in honor of Kareem Abdul-Jabbar. The No. 34 jersey was also chosen in honor of his stepfather, who wore that number in the Army.


First two seasons (1996–1998)
The Lakers won 56 games during the 1996–97 season. O'Neal averaged 26.2 points and 12.5 rebounds in his first season with the team, but missed over 30 games due to injuries. The Lakers made the playoffs, but were eliminated in the second round by the Utah Jazz in five games. In his first playoff game for the Lakers, O'Neal scored 46 points against the Portland Trail Blazers, the most for a Lakers player in a playoff game since Jerry West's 53 points in 1969. On December 17, 1996, O'Neal shoved Dennis Rodman of the Chicago Bulls; the Los Angeles Daily News later reported that O'Neal was willing to be suspended for fighting Rodman.
During the 1997–98 season, O'Neal averaged 28.3 points and 11.4 rebounds with a 58.4 field goal percentage. It was the first of four consecutive seasons in which he led the league in field goal percentage. The Lakers finished the season 61–21, first in the Pacific Division, and were the second seed in the Western Conference during the 1998 NBA Playoffs. After defeating the Portland Trail Blazers and Seattle SuperSonics in the first two rounds, the Lakers again lost to the Jazz, this time in a 4–0 sweep.


O'Neal–Bryant tandem buildup (1998–1999)
With the tandem of O'Neal and the Lakers' teenage superstar Kobe Bryant, expectations for the team increased, although personnel changes led to instability during the 1998–99 season. The Lakers traded long-time point guard Nick Van Exel to the Denver Nuggets, and acquired Glen Rice from the Charlotte Hornets to satisfy O'Neal's demand for a strong shooter. Coach Del Harris was fired, and former Lakers forward Kurt Rambis finished the season as head coach. The Lakers finished with a 31–19 record during the lockout-shortened season. Although they made the playoffs, they were swept by the San Antonio Spurs, led by Tim Duncan and David Robinson, in the second round of the Western Conference playoffs.


MVP and championship seasons (1999–2002)
Before the 1999–2000 season, the Lakers hired Phil Jackson as head coach. During a game against the Houston Rockets in November 1999, O'Neal blocked a layup by the Rockets' Charles Barkley. O'Neal then shoved Barkley, who responded by throwing the ball at O'Neal; both players were ejected from the game. grok_lead: Shaquille Rashaun O'Neal, commonly known as Shaq, is an American former professional basketball player widely regarded as one of the most dominant centers in National Basketball Association (NBA) history. Born on March 6, 1972, in Newark, New Jersey, O'Neal stands at 7 feet 1 inch (2.16 m) tall and weighed 325 pounds (147 kg) during his playing career, using his immense size and athleticism to average 23.7 points, 10.9 rebounds, and 2.5 assists over 1,207 games across 19 seasons with six teams: the Orlando Magic, Los Angeles Lakers, Miami Heat, Phoenix Suns, Cleveland Cavaliers, and Boston Celtics. Drafted first overall by the Magic in 1992 after a standout college career at Louisiana State University, where he was named National Player of the Year in 1992, O'Neal earned NBA Rookie of the Year honors in 1993 and quickly established himself as a force, leading the league in scoring average twice and ranking among the all-time leaders in points (11th), field goals made (eighth), and field goal percentage (15th at 58.2%). O'Neal's pinnacle achievements came during his eight seasons with the Lakers from 1996 to 2004, where he formed a dynasty with Kobe Bryant, securing three consecutive NBA championships (2000â2002) and earning three Finals MVP awards in those years, along with the league MVP in 2000. His fourth championship followed in 2006 with the Heat, solidifying his legacy with 15 All-Star selections, three All-Star Game MVPs, 14 All-NBA honors (eight First Team), and three All-Defensive Team nods. Internationally, O'Neal contributed to the U.S. Olympic team's gold medal at the 1996 Atlanta Games. Inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 2016, he was also selected to the NBA's 50th and 75th Anniversary Teams, recognizing his transformative impact on the game through sheer physical dominance and scoring prowess around the basket. Beyond basketball, O'Neal has built a multifaceted career in entertainment, business, and philanthropy. He has appeared in films and television, released platinum-selling rap albums like Shaq Diesel (1993), and served as a studio analyst on TNT's Inside the NBA since 2008, earning widespread acclaim for his charismatic commentary. In business, O'Neal is a prolific entrepreneur with investments in franchises like Papa John's (where he was a board member until 2020), ownership stakes in the Sacramento Kings (2013â2022) and Kings Guard Gaming in the NBA 2K League, and recent ventures including a role as President of Reebok Basketball (announced 2024), partnerships with JCPenney in beauty products (2025), and founding partner in Jacmel Infrastructure (2025). As a philanthropist, he has been the national spokesperson for the Boys & Girls Clubs of America for over 15 years and supported various youth and education initiatives. In 2025, O'Neal took on the role of general manager for the Sacramento State men's basketball program, further extending his influence in the sport.
